title: Review: industry growth and political spending
document_type: Internal research-design review note (self-described as not an empirical result; no models estimated)
coverage: Full text read in one pass (30,563 chars, 221 lines): front matter, overall verdict, risk ranking, starting formula, sections 1-14, data and citation corrections table, literature list, design steps. No _annots files exist (annot_sha12s empty), so paul_markup is empty. Author taken from metadata per note:true instruction; the text itself names no author and reviews a brief titled Astra_Review_Brief_Sector_Growth_and_Political_Spending.md. Cited URLs were not fetched; claims are taken as stated in the text. Metadata title and venue judged correct. key_findings capped at 12 of 13 candidates; dropped the Section 12 policy-salience finding (hearing-count control; catalog listed through 2021, which is in limitations).
research_question: Does prior-year real industry growth predict subsequent organizational political spending (corporate and trade-association PAC contributions to congressional candidates, and reported LDA lobbying expenditure), and do election expectations (probability of chamber control) predict where PAC giving goes across parties, incumbents and committee members? The growth association is the main question; expectations are a separate, exploratory question.
theory: Three mechanisms, not a predetermined sign: favorable performance can expand capacity; poor performance can raise demand for relief while reducing resources; threatened policy losses can induce spending in either economic state. Majority status has value (Cox and Magar). Committee access drives reallocation (Powell and Grimmer). Regulatory shocks can lower output and raise lobbying at once, producing a negative association without distress-driven behavior.
data: Not yet assembled; no N estimated. Unit: industry-year. Case analysis uses five sectors; broad panel may use five to ten sectors or all insurance carriers. Proposed common panel 2008-2024 (about 18 annual observations; 2025 only after source audit). Outcomes: FEC committee-to-candidate PAC disbursements (DIME v4.0 covers 1979-2024 public itemized files, excluding CRP/NIMSP-sourced records); LDA LD-2 lobbying, quarterly from 2008. Growth: BEA real value added. Expectations: chamber-control markets (Iowa Electronic Markets, incomplete odd-year coverage) or archived forecasts, about nine elections, six realized chamber flips. Salience: Policy Agendas hearings catalog (listed through 2021) and Unified Agenda editions.
method: Main model: log S_it = alpha_i + lambda_t + beta g_{i,t-1} + e, with sector and year effects, estimated separately for PAC contributions and lobbying (never summed). Growth g = 100 (V_t / V_{t-1} - 1) on raw real value added. Alternatives: PPML exponential conditional mean if genuine zeros exist; log initial sector size at t-2 as a control; split growth into g+ = max(g,0) and g- = max(-g,0) for asymmetry; dynamic FE only as sensitivity (Bruno bias correction; Arellano-Bond or system GMM not recommended with five to ten sectors). Expectations study: RShare = sector/chamber baseline + coefficient times earlier P + coefficient times current control + limited calendar controls, with a fractional-response sensitivity. Inference: small-sample cluster corrections, restricted wild-cluster bootstrap, cluster leverage, leave-one-sector-out, Driscoll-Kraay only as sensitivity, randomization inference only with a defensible assignment argument.
identification: Identification rests on within-sector variation in lagged real growth net of sector means and common year shocks. Lagging fixes ordering but does not establish causality; the Bruno correction does not solve endogeneity in current-year growth. Expectations identification comes from election-cycle variation in earlier control probabilities, with roughly nine elections and six realized flips, so the review treats those estimates as exploratory. Chamber-by-year effects absorb chamber-specific probabilities in a pooled panel.
measures: Spending: inflation-adjusted PAC contributions and lobbying expenditure (logs). Growth: raw percent change in BEA real value added; standardized growth only as secondary presentation. P: earlier probability of Republican chamber control. M: current Republican control. RShare: Republican share of candidate giving (undefined when total partisan giving is zero). Secondary: incumbent share, committee-member share, expected seat change, lagged count of relevant congressional hearings, pending regulatory proceedings (sensitivity).
scope: Prospective design for US federal politics: corporate and trade-association PAC disbursements to congressional candidates, LDA lobbying, BEA-classified industries, 2008-2024 (2025 if audited). Excludes unregistered advocacy, state politics, and industry-affiliated individual giving, party contributions, super PAC financing and independent expenditures, which are to be analyzed as separate channels.

key_findings.finding: Make prior real industry growth the main analysis; treat election expectations and partisan allocation as a separate, more exploratory analysis because more industries add information about growth but not more national elections.
key_findings.numbers: No estimates; 14 numbered sections of recommendations

key_findings.finding: The measures (asset growth, profits, premiums, production, crypto valuations) do not yet share a common economic mechanism; z-scores change scale, not meaning.
Repeating a national forecast across industries adds no independent forecast shocks; coverage, timing, common shocks and roughly nine elections matter more than total row count.
Shift plus current control is a reparameterization of probability plus current control; the current-control coefficient holding P fixed is g minus f.
key_findings.location: Section 4, equation after 'Use P and current control directly'

key_findings.finding: A contraction indicator is not an asymmetric slope; define contraction on raw real growth below zero and use g+ and g- with separate coefficients to test asymmetry.
Majority status has value: Cox and Magar estimate an approximately 36,000 dollar majority premium around the 1994 House switch, but this does not establish a response speed to forecast changes.
Illustration only: beta of 0.03 would correspond to about 3.05 percent higher typical spending per one-point growth increase, computed as 100(e^beta - 1); this is not an estimated result.
key_findings.location: Overall formula section, paragraph on interpretation

key_findings.finding: Corporate PAC donations come from voluntary segregated funds, so a direct financial-capacity mechanism fits lobbying more naturally than PAC donations; PAC profits are not the contribution budget.
In-house lobbying totals can double-count retained-firm payments and association dues; use documented deduplication and report trade-association totals separately or with an overlap adjustment.
No seamless 2008-2025 probability series is verified; build a chamber-by-election inventory and leave unavailable IEM observations missing rather than filling with 0.5 or actual results.

Fairshake receipts are not outside spending; the FEC table reports about 260.071 million dollars receipts, 195.827 million disbursements and 40.662 million direct independent expenditures for Fairshake itself, with related committees needing consolidation.
key_findings.location: Data and citation corrections table, row 5

key_findings.finding: Keep life insurance as a federal case with exclusion sensitivity; state data added only for insurers would change outcome scope, and broad insurance growth must not be labeled life-insurance growth.

limitations: Design review only: no models estimated and no panel assembled; numbers are documentary or illustrative.
Claims about the OpenSecrets API end date (April 15, 2025) and bulk access could not be verified from primary pages and are treated as unconfirmed.
DIME public itemized files exclude CRP/NIMSP-sourced records; separate academic request needed for those.
The 538 generic-ballot historical CSV covers November 1995 to November 2016 and is not a contemporaneous forecast archive.
Policy Agendas hearing catalog is incomplete and listed through 2021 only.
Roughly nine elections and six realized chamber flips limit the expectations analysis; results would be exploratory.
With five sectors and 18 annual observations, bootstrap and Driscoll-Kraay inference are unreliable; cluster corrections also have limits.
Registered lobbying does not capture unregistered advocacy; a registration drop does not mechanically imply lower political effort.
Fairshake related committees require separate consolidation before totals are used.
